title: PR #211 — replace N+1 in invoice loader with a lateral join
body: The invoice list endpoint was issuing one query per line item. I replaced the N+1 in the invoice loader with a lateral join and pushed the aggregation into Postgres. p95 on /v2/invoices went from 1.9s to 240ms on the staging dataset (2.4M rows). Added an EXPLAIN ANALYZE regression test so this cannot silently come back.

title: ENG-884 — settlement report times out for large merchants
body: Root cause was a missing index. Added a partial index on events(tenant_id, created_at) WHERE kind = 'settlement', which cut the report query from 34s to 1.1s for our largest merchant. Documented why a partial index beats a composite here given the 4% selectivity.

title: perf: batch the payout reconciliation writes
body: Rewrote the reconciliation writer in Python to use COPY instead of row-by-row inserts. 40k payouts now reconcile in 9s rather than 6 minutes.

title: Design doc — zero-downtime migration of the ledger to partitioned tables
body: Proposal to move the ledger_entries table (890M rows) to declarative partitioning by month. Covers the dual-write window, the backfill ordering, how we verify parity with a checksum job, and the rollback path at each of the five cutover stages. Reviewed by Priya and Gil; approved with one change to the verification step.

title: PR #260 — dual-write ledger entries behind a flag
body: First stage of the partitioning migration. Dual-writes to both the old and new ledger tables behind LEDGER_PARTITION_DUALWRITE, with a shadow-read comparator that logs divergence instead of failing the request. 11 integration tests covering the divergence paths.

title: PR #288 — backfill job for 890M ledger rows
body: Chunked backfill with resumable checkpoints, throttled against replica lag. Ran over nine nights with zero customer-facing errors; I held the pager for each window. Parity checksum matched on all 890M rows before we flipped reads.

title: Manager feedback — Nour Haddad
body: Maya led the ledger partitioning end to end: the design doc, the staged rollout and the comms to the merchant-support team. She coordinated three engineers across Payments and Data Platform without being asked to, and the migration landed with no incidents. Growth area: she is still reluctant to hand work off, and took on the backfill nights herself rather than sharing the rota.

title: INC-412 — sev1: payout webhooks stalled for 38 minutes
body: I was primary on-call. Diagnosed a connection-pool exhaustion caused by a slow downstream PSP call holding transactions open. Mitigated by moving the PSP call outside the transaction boundary and shipping a pool-saturation alert. Wrote the postmortem and drove all four action items to done.

title: Postmortem — INC-412 payout webhook stall
body: Timeline, contributing factors and corrections. Key finding: we had no alert on connection-pool saturation despite it being the failure mode of the previous two sev2s. Added a Prometheus rule plus a dashboard panel, and added the saturation metric to the payments service SLO review.

title: obs: add OpenTelemetry spans across the settlement path
body: Instrumented the settlement pipeline with OpenTelemetry spans so we can attribute latency between our code and the PSP. Trace-based p99 attribution now shows 71% of settlement latency is downstream.

title: PR #341 — v2 payouts API with idempotency keys
body: Designed and shipped the v2 payouts interface. Idempotency keys with a 24h replay window, RFC 7807 problem details for errors, and cursor pagination rather than offset. Wrote the OpenAPI spec first and generated the client from it so the mobile team was unblocked before the server landed.

title: Peer feedback — Priya Ramanathan
body: Maya's v2 payouts spec was the cleanest interface proposal I have reviewed here. She pushed back on my suggestion to expose the internal settlement state machine and she was right to; the resulting API is much harder to misuse.

title: ENG-1019 — reconciliation mismatch with card network file format
body: Card network changed the fixed-width layout of the daily settlement file without notice. Wrote a tolerant parser with explicit column versioning, plus a reconciliation report that flags unmatched rows by reason code rather than dumping them into one bucket.

title: Data model — merchant payout aggregates
body: Dimensional model for merchant payout reporting: a daily grain fact table, three conformed dimensions, and late-arriving-fact handling for settlements that land after the reporting window closes. Chose a Type 2 dimension for merchant risk tier because finance needs to reproduce historical reports exactly.

title: test: property-based tests for the currency rounding helpers
body: Replaced 40 hand-written example tests with a Python Hypothesis property suite. It immediately found a half-cent rounding drift on JPY, which has no minor unit.

title: bump replica count for payments-api
body: Scaled the payments-api deployment from 6 to 9 replicas ahead of the quarter-end settlement peak.

title: ENG-1102 — GDPR erasure request handling for payout records
body: Implemented erasure for personal fields on payout records while retaining the financial record required for our seven-year retention obligation. Worked with legal to agree which fields are personal data and which are transaction records. Added an audit entry for every erasure so we can evidence compliance.

title: Manager feedback — Nour Haddad
body: Another strong half. Maya is the person the team routes hard database and correctness problems to. She has started reviewing Hana's pull requests carefully and explaining the reasoning rather than just approving, which Hana has told me is the most useful onboarding she has had. Next step for Maya is scope beyond Payments: she has not yet worked on anything streaming or event-driven, which is where most of our platform investment is going.

title: PR #402 — make the settlement importer resumable
body: The Python importer previously restarted from zero on failure. Now it checkpoints per file chunk in Postgres and resumes. Cut a recurring 3am page down to an automatic recovery.

title: docs: runbook for settlement file ingestion failures
body: Wrote the runbook the on-call actually needs: the four failure modes we have seen, how to tell them apart from the dashboard, and the exact remediation for each.

title: INC-501 — sev2: duplicate payouts to 214 merchants
body: Shadowed on-call for this one. Traced duplicates to a retry without an idempotency key in an internal batch tool, not the v2 API. Wrote the reversal script and reconciled all 214 accounts. Then removed the entire class of bug by making the internal tool go through the v2 idempotent endpoint.

title: RFC — should Payments own its settlement event stream?
body: I do not have production streaming experience, so this RFC is deliberately framed as questions rather than a recommendation. Lays out three options for getting settlement events to Data Platform, the ordering guarantees each would give us, and what I would need to learn to own option two. Asking for a reviewer from Data Platform.

title: AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional
body: Certification record. Maya Reyes holds AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional, issued 11 June 2025, valid through 11 June 2028. Verification code SAP-2025-0611-MR. This certification covers architecture design, migration planning and cost optimisation.

title: Structured reference check — Nour Haddad
body: Asked to confirm scope and reporting line. Maya reported to me for two years as an individual contributor. She did not have direct reports at any point and was not in the management chain. On the ledger partitioning she coordinated three engineers as the technical lead of that project, which is the largest span she has held. She reviewed pull requests for one junior engineer, Hana, over about six months. She was primary on-call for payments on a six-week rotation. I would hire her again without hesitation.

title: Structured reference check — Priya Ramanathan
body: Asked specifically about streaming and event infrastructure. Maya has not worked on our streaming systems. She wrote a thoughtful RFC asking what it would take to own one, which is how I know she understands the problem, but she has never run a Kafka consumer in production here. On Postgres she is the strongest person on the payments team and I have taken her review on partitioning decisions for my own work.

title: Q3 cost review — platform estate
body: Cloud spend for the platform estate fell from $2.41M to $1.49M over the fiscal year, a 38% reduction. The largest single contributor was moving stateless workloads to spot capacity with a drain controller, followed by rightsizing 180 over-provisioned pod specs and deleting 31 idle load balancers. Devika owned this programme end to end.

title: PR #88 — spot capacity with a drain controller
body: Moves stateless workloads onto spot instances behind a drain controller that cordons and reschedules on the two-minute interruption notice. Tested against simulated reclaim at 5x normal rate with no dropped requests.

title: PLAT-207 — rightsize over-provisioned pod specs
body: Audited every deployment against 30-day p95 utilisation and corrected 180 pod specs. Requests were on average 3.4x actual usage. No latency regression on any service after rollout.

title: Terraform module library — migration plan
body: Plan to move 40 services off hand-rolled deploy scripts onto a shared Terraform module library. Covers module boundaries, state layout per environment, and the sequencing so no service is half-migrated across a release.

title: PR #142 — terraform module library, first 12 services
body: First tranche of the migration. Twelve services now provision through the shared modules with per-environment state. Drift detection runs nightly and opens a ticket rather than auto-applying.

title: PLAT-388 — terraform migration complete
body: All 40 services are now provisioned through the module library. Hand-rolled deploy scripts deleted. Mean time to stand up a new service environment went from two days to under an hour.

title: Service inventory — production estate
body: Canonical inventory, regenerated nightly from the service registry. The estate currently comprises 43 production services across 7 teams. Counting every ephemeral preview environment would inflate this number considerably, which is why this document counts registered production services only.

title: Design — multi-region failover for the payments estate
body: Author: Arjun Desai. Reviewers: Devika Nair, Priyanka Iyer. Proposes active-passive failover across two regions with a controlled promotion path and a documented data-loss budget. Devika's review raised the split-brain risk during partial network partition, which changed the promotion design.

title: PR #201 — game day harness for region failover
body: Harness to run quarterly failover game days: severs inter-region traffic, drives promotion, measures recovery. Devika ran the first three game days and wrote up each one.

title: PR #96 — connection pooling in the API gateway
body: Adds keep-alive connection pooling between the gateway and upstream services. p99 on the gateway went from 420ms to 273ms under production replay. Further gains would need upstream changes we do not own.

title: Incident review — H2 2025 platform reliability
body: Median time to recovery across platform incidents moved from 45 minutes to 22 over the half. The largest contributors were the runbook index and paging the owning team directly rather than routing everything through platform on-call.

title: INC-618 — sev1: control plane unavailable for 26 minutes
body: Devika was incident commander. Root cause was etcd disk saturation on two of three control plane nodes after a log-level change shipped without review. Mitigated by raising the disk tier and adding a pre-merge check on log-level changes.

title: Internal developer platform — adoption review
body: The internal developer platform has been adopted by three of the five engineering teams. Payments and Growth are still on the legacy pipeline; Payments has a migration scheduled, Growth has not committed. Adoption stalled on the lack of a migration path for services with custom build steps.

title: PR #57 — golden path service scaffold
body: One command to scaffold a service with CI, observability, deploy config and an on-call rota entry already wired. Reduced the new-service checklist from 23 manual steps to 3.

title: obs: SLO burn-rate alerts for every tier-1 service
body: Replaces threshold alerts with multi-window burn-rate alerts on the published SLOs. Paging volume on tier-1 services dropped by roughly half with no increase in missed incidents.

title: PLAT-451 — Python tooling for drift reconciliation
body: Wrote the reconciler in Python: diffs live cloud state against Terraform state, classifies drift as benign or material, and files a ticket for material drift with the offending resource and owner.

title: go: rewrite the drain controller hot path
body: Rewrote the drain controller's reconcile loop in Go after the Python prototype could not keep up with reclaim bursts. Handles 400 evictions per minute with headroom.

title: Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA)
body: Certification record. Devika Nair passed Certified Kubernetes Administrator on 14 March 2021. This certification was valid through 14 March 2024 and has since expired. It has not been renewed. Verification ID CKA-2021-0314-DN.

source: Referee — Rahul Menon, Director of Engineering
title: Structured reference check — Rahul Menon
body: Asked to confirm scope and ownership. Devika is a staff individual contributor. She led the platform working group, which is six engineers drawn from three teams — a working group, not a reporting line; nobody reports to her. The cost programme was hers outright and the numbers in the Q3 review are correct. I would want to be precise about the multi-region failover: that design was Arjun's. Devika reviewed it, and her review changed the promotion path, and she ran the game days. She did not architect it.

title: Structured reference check — Priyanka Iyer
body: Asked specifically about data and streaming work. Devika has not worked on our streaming or analytics systems at all — that is a different team and she has never been on it. On infrastructure she is the person I would want on any Kubernetes or Terraform problem, and the drain controller was genuinely clever work.

title: Working group charter — platform enablement
body: The platform working group is six engineers seconded part-time from three teams, chaired by Devika Nair. It has no reporting line and no budget; it sets platform standards and reviews platform-adjacent designs.

title: PLAT-502 — decommission 31 idle load balancers
body: Identified load balancers with no traffic for 90 days and removed them after owner sign-off. Saved roughly $7.4k per month.
